requirements.name: tools-sidebar explorer entry with focused overlay
key UX: The File Explorer still launches from the Tools sidebar and keeps the existing workspace gating logic.
Opening the explorer closes competing overlays and brings up a dedicated explorer surface instead of a cramped utility pane feel.
The new UI keeps the old open and close behavior, but visually frames the explorer as a primary workspace task.

requirements.name: mobile-first single-focus layout
key UX: The explorer now uses one single mobile-first flow across screen sizes instead of keeping a separate desktop split-pane logic.
Folder browsing, file preview, and file editing are distinct full-surface states so the user focuses on one task at a time.
The UI no longer expands into a desktop-specific dual-pane layout; the same single-column navigation model is reused everywhere.

requirements.name: header with breadcrumb path and clear session actions
key UX: The top area now switches between a close action for the file list and a Back action for file detail states, with the current file context in the center.
Breadcrumb navigation remains available for folder browsing, but file detail actions such as Edit and Preview are anchored in the header instead of sharing space with the list.
Primary actions such as close, return to files, and edit or save are anchored in predictable header or footer positions.

requirements.name: icon-led directory and file list
key UX: Folder and file rows are now distinguished primarily through icons rather than literal `[dir]` or `[file]` labels.
Each row remains a full-width tap target and still maps to the same old behavior: folders navigate deeper and files attempt to open.
List rows stay on one line and only show compact supporting metadata such as size and non-default file state like read-only, instead of repeating type information from the filename.

requirements.name: existing workspace-rooted navigation logic with cleaner hierarchy
key UX: The explorer still opens at workspace root and still supports entering folders and going upward through the current path hierarchy.
The Up behavior and workspace-relative path logic remain unchanged, but the UI presents parent navigation as part of the list and breadcrumb hierarchy.
Empty folders, loading states, and load failures are shown as deliberate explorer states instead of feeling like missing layout.

requirements.name: preview-first file detail flow using old open rules
key UX: The current file-open rules stay intact, but the UI now moves from the file list into a dedicated preview screen before the user enters editing.
Supported text files still open with filename, encoding, and content, yet the new layout treats file detail as a focused reading and editing surface rather than a side pane.
The explorer no longer shows the file list and editor together; returning from preview or edit goes back to the list flow.

requirements.name: editability gating preserved with clearer visual states
key UX: The allowlist logic for editable files remains exactly the same, including supported config and text formats and the existing v1 limitations.
Files that are visible but not editable are presented with a clear read-only visual state instead of blending into editable entries.
This keeps the old backend and frontend capability boundaries while making the UI honest about what can and cannot be edited.

requirements.name: too-large and unsupported fallback logic with better state screens
key UX: The old fallback behavior for unsupported or oversized files remains in place, including the 256 KB size limit.
The UI now expresses these outcomes as explicit single-purpose state screens tied to the target file context instead of feeling like an abrupt generic fallback.
Users can return to the file list directly from these state screens without the old split-pane mental model.

requirements.name: sticky save flow and visible dirty state
key UX: The old save behavior stays unchanged: only existing editable files can be saved, and Save enables only when the draft is dirty and a save is not already running.
The redesigned UI gives unsaved changes a stronger visual presence through a persistent dirty indicator and a fixed bottom action area in edit mode.
Successful saves still update local state and file size while keeping the user inside the focused preview/edit flow.

requirements.name: unchanged unsaved-change protection with calmer exit affordances
key UX: The current protection logic remains the same when the user closes the explorer, opens another file, or navigates away with unsaved changes.
The new UI makes the risk more visible before the user hits the blocking confirm step, so the browser confirmation is no longer the only signal.
This preserves the old guardrails while making accidental loss of edits feel less abrupt.

requirements.name: chat-linked file opening with integrated explorer context
key UX: The existing `file://` handoff logic from chat remains unchanged and still rejects targets outside the active workspace.
The redesigned UI opens linked folders and files inside the same focused explorer flow, so chat-origin navigation feels native instead of bolted on.
Linked file opens still honor the same editable, unsupported, too-large, and outside-workspace rules as direct explorer navigation.

requirements.name: tolerant AI-generated path recognition for file jumps
key UX: File jump parsing should become more tolerant of AI-generated path variants, including unstable `file://` prefixes, mixed slash styles, encoded separators such as `%5C`, and lightly wrapped path text.
The resolver should normalize noisy path strings into a stable workspace-relative target before deciding whether to open a folder or file.
Recognition should become smarter without weakening safety: ambiguous or outside-workspace targets must still be rejected instead of guessing aggressively.

requirements.name: workspace safety and race handling preserved behind the new UI
key UX: The redesign does not change the existing workspace-boundary protections, symlink filtering, or path validation rules.
The redesign also keeps the current race-safe async behavior where only the latest request is allowed to win.
Visually the explorer feels cleaner and more intentional, but its underlying safety model and state consistency rules remain the old ones.
